If you enjoyed Hypnospace outlaw or other similar games, or enjoy the x files, I think you'll enjoy this.

review_text_raw:
My recommendation is heavily conditional. If you are into conspiracies and point-and-click games with simple puzzle elements, I would recommend this at around $10. If you don't fall into those categories, then you aren't the target demographic and I can't recommend it. Overall Operator is not a bad game - in fact, I would really like to see more content for this, or perhaps even more games like it - but it's held back by a few flaws.

First, The Good:
[list]
    [*]The setting and overall theme is great. You play as a deskbound investigator at the not-FBI, using your computer to sift through clues and work with field agents to investigate crimes. Naturally, this leads to uncovering conspiracies and shadowy organizations.
    [*]The gameplay is intuitive and accessible. You will never have to pixel-hunt for your clues; when you're inspecting a piece of evidence, the things that your gut tell you are important to the case usually are, and they're usually clickable.
    [*]The story is fun, interesting, and will keep you engaged. It references some real-world "conspiracies" that actually happened.
    [*]The gameplay loop feels fresh. I know games in this format have been done before, but it's been a while since I've seen it executed like this. I don't know of many recent games that are quite like it.
[/list]

Next, The Bad:
[list]
    [*]The puzzles are a bit simple. At times it feels like more of a visual novel than a detective/investigation game.
    [*]Many of the plot twists are predictable. The dramatic reveals towards the end of the game didn't land with me at all because I had already seen them coming way ahead of time.
    [*]Sometimes there are clues that fall into your lap a little too easily, to the point where it doesn't feel believable. The most egregious example: [spoiler]During one investigation, you find the buried body of a scientist who worked on a secret government project. The people involved with the project had him killed to keep him quiet. For some reason, they buried him in a marked grave, near the marked graves of a hundred of the project's victims, wearing his full lab coat, with his work ID showing full name and place of employment still in a cord around his neck, and with unwiped floppy disks in his pocket that contained all of his research and notes.[/spoiler]
    [*]The game is filled with anachronisms. It's supposed to be set in 1992, but it doesn't even attempt to maintain this setting. Everybody has a cell phone, which in the 90s were expensive, rare, and had very limited coverage; the computer used by main character appears to have a multi-core CPU, which didn't exist until the 2000s; and one of the early investigations involves a digital camera with a large preview screen, which also did not exist in 1992. All of this is like having a character use an iPhone in a video game about Operation Desert Storm; it can be immersion-breaking. Operator probably should have been set in the mid- to late-2000s, not 1992.
    [*]At the time of writing, there is only one ending, and it feels rushed. [spoiler]Outside of one minor detail regarding a side character, your choices don't matter.[/spoiler]
    [*]The last and most obvious drawback is probably the one you've seen mentioned in other reviews: this is a short game. It'll probably only take you around 3 hours to complete. The cynic in me wonders if this was done intentionally to get around the 2-hour Steam refund limit.
[/list]

I did enjoy my time with Operator; if you're like me, and enjoy the thought of playing detective and uncovering government conspiracies, you probably will too. Ultimately I think this is a decent game with a solid concept behind it, but the problems I listed above hold me back from recommending this unconditionally. In particular, I feel that Operator is slightly overpriced when measured against the amount of gameplay time you're likely to get out of it. This seems to be the developer's first game, so I'm hoping that they take the lessons learned from Operator and continue to improve on this formula.

review_text_raw:
The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

Rating: 9/10

review_text_raw:
Played the demo and got really hooked, so I bought the game the next day full price.

AFTER the demo I expected it to be very similar to Orville and Cyber Manhunt, with the primary focus on using the game's mechanics to solve multiple criminal cases, most unrelated or maybe filler and some interconnected into a bigger picture.
It was... kinda like that? But instead of a focus on multiple cases and the solving mechanics, it focuses solely on one storyline.

Which to me was actually really sad I guess because the gameplay mechanics were really well implemented and would have made for a super nice gameplay loop but instead got used once to advance the plot and then got discarded (e.g. the lab analysis or manually unlocking files). 

Also, the game is probably 75% dialogue, in which you are given choices that lead nowhere. You feel like your choices should matter, maybe in resulting in different endings but there is only one ending implemented. It actually made me compare it more to a visual novel than a detective game.

The lack of "filler cases" is also more of a negative in this particular storyline. I've read that the developer wanted to focus more on the main story instead of filler but I think some filler would've helped the player to immerse themselves better into their role, made better usage of the well-implemented mechanics and would've allowed the player to connect with the characters better, settle mentally on the twists and turns of the main story and process them before the next thing gets thrown at them. It felt very fast-paced with no breathing time from basically the get-go and if I'm not mistaken the story takes place within only a couple of days in-game which also does not seem realistic.

Conclusion:
+ well-made from a technical point of view
+ well implemented mechanics
+ good soundtrack
- poor use of mechanics
- unclear advertisement (detective game vs. very story-driven, more of a visual novel)
- no actual choices made by the player even though it feels like they should have mattered
- lack of cases with a rather short gameplay time as a result
- lots of dialogue with comparatively little gameplay

If you're looking for somethin akin to Orville, Cyber Manhunt or even Her Story, this is not it.
I considered requesting a refund but I believe that if I buy a product, receive it and use it, there is no reason in refunding it, even if it was not what I expected

review_text_raw:
This game only has one ending, and only less than 2½ - 3 hours of content in total, making the cost per played hour very high. 
The one singular ending is quite bad, and even though there are many dialogue options, there are no actual meaningful choices to be made.
There are numerous quite long and somewhat boring unskippable cut scenes. However one could argue that having no skip option is acceptable due to it being somewhat important to pay attention to the them. And since there's only one ending, there's no replayability, and so there's no need to have a skip option. Though realistically, and as others have pointed out, the most probable reason for not having a skip option is to extend the required playtime to over 2 hours so the game cannot be refunded through Steam.
The game has a lot of dialogue, and not a lot of gameplay. What little actual gameplay there is, is enjoyable enough I guess, but also pretty simplistic and easy. This can be seen as both a positive and a negative. If you're looking for any sort of a challenge/puzzle, you will not find it in this game. This game should be definitely thought of as a visual novel more than a puzzle game.
The story itself is mediocre and actually pretty shallow, which is very bad for a game that consists mainly of the story.
The dialogue is fully voice-acted (except for [spoiler]HAL[/spoiler] and the protagonist), which is a definite plus. The voice acting is also pretty high-quality. However I cannot help but feel like way too much developer effort and money was put into the voice acting, when it should've been put into other aspects of the game.
The soundscape and the soundtrack are also good, but really nothing out of the ordinary.

Overall, The Operator is a short, pricey mediocre dialogue-heavy and minimal-gameplay game with high-quality voice acting and heavy hand-holding and railroading, and with only one ending. It feels like the game was designed to be just long enough to make it impossible to refund after reaching the ending (which in fairness one shouldn't do regardless, if they enjoyed the game and reached the ending).

I cannot recommend anything else but to watch someone else such as a YouTuber play this game. I think that will actually add way more to the experience than buying the game and playing it on your own.

Has promise, but doesn't deliver.

Mechanically there are a handful of things that seem interesting and like you should pay attention to them that just don't go anywhere. There is no real point in taking notes because you are handed solutions to every problem without needing to look around or remember anything.

Cool, I can run programs from my terminal - [spoiler] e.g. I can call certain people if I pay attention to their IP addresses [/spoiler]. But does that come up at all after I'm shown it? No, it's a one-off to get my to type something into the terminal for vibes. Problems are not solveable outside of the linear storyline. Problems and solutions are presented to you side by side. There is no payoff for paying attention to details, because they don't go anywhere, you can't use them to figure anything out. Very much on rails, and a disappointing detective game experience. I almost thought this would go somewhere cool at the end [spoiler] and that you would continue the game as HAL and actually find out who the mysterious baddies are [/spoiler], but this too does not pay off. Just leaves me wanting more, but not in a good way; feels almost like a demo. When it was revealed [spoiler] who the mole was I was like yeah, ok, there are like 6 total people I have met who aren't dead, of course it's my sketchy friend Mike who's been acting weird. [/spoiler]

That being said, individual minigames and puzzles were genuinely fun to solve. I wish the game leaned more into the mechanics and systems they had, I think that is where they were strongest, and made it important and useful to take notes - reward paying attention to the details! Why give us a notepad if there's nothing you realistically need to write down? I wish I like this game more!

The Operator is an indie underrated gem. The art and design are immaculate, and the problem-solving challenge is manageable - not completely mindboggling but not spoonfeeding you the answers either.

Unfortunately I'm not a big fan of cliffhanger bleak endings, and I also believe this game's story would be much richer with multiple endings and a few more side-cases. 

Regardless, a good 4-6 hour leisurely play with a unreached potential.

Conspiratorial thinking is kinda like anime girls. Like, okay. So there's this super hot princess from planet catgirl who's on the run from the space mafia, and she just so happens to teleport naked right into your bathtub. While you're in it. And because of this, she's super into you for some reason. Yeah, sounds nice, but this is so insanely removed from how actual relationships form, it's like watching aliens mate (I mean... she is an alien, so...)

And with conspiracies it's like: okay, so there's this ultra-powerful cabal of politicians, billionaires and celebrities, who completely control the society without being spotted... but then they reveal themselves by using symbols in plain sight. And the person to stop them? A bumbling born-into-wealth TV-star who in fact is a 5D-chess player, so all his obvious mistakes are actually genius moves that you just don't get. I don't know guys, seems very legit, but there are a few pieces of this story that make me question its validity.

Think about how a real conspiracy of this scale would work. Incomprehensible wealth would be poured into world-class assassins and operatives to ensure compliance or silence. Evidence would be erased with brutal efficiency, with red herrings and multiple layers of scapegoats; but even then, people are people, and eventually something could possibly slip the cracks. 

The Operator explores this more realistic portrayal of conspiracies, with the scale also being somewhat more realistic. You don't know who you can trust and who you can't. But not everyone (except you) is in on it.

Right?

But hold on. Before you start yelling LOOMINARTY CONFIRMED and smoking dat 420 MLG style, some actual work needs to be done. You're an [strike]FBI[/strike] FDI operator with an access to a pretty sweet database, but also a job to do - to support agents in the field. Whatever confirming of loominarty you'll be doing will have to be squeezed in between protecting and serving those who [strike]are supposed to[/strike] protect and serve. review_text_raw:
I have to say I was absolutely hooked with the concept of [i] The Operator. [/i] One watch of the trailer will tell you why; an operator helping with government investigations, analyzing clues, basically being the man-in-the-chair? It's all awesome! But what killed the mood for me was the cliche writing, amateur voice acting, and the simplistic puzzles. First of all the writing. Who TALKS like this?! Every person you meet is quippy, chippy, or clever with their line delivery. These don't sound like professional field agents, they sound like cartoon characters. A man has been killed, TAKE THIS SERIOUSLY! They should be more realistic, a bit grittier, more direct. And why am I doing everything? What exactly is your job here??

Next are the puzzles. They are already simple enough, but I feel babied and talked down to by the characters we meet. The game would make itself so much more compelling if there were harder applications! Something I had to grill through to find what my agent needed. So far, I can click two buttons and get the answer to the riddle. I don't [i] feel [/i] like a secret agent, which is what I bought the game for. And not to mention the game's animations for security footage, which are taken so seriously for how poor in quality they are. The tone simply doesn't match. 

Finally, I had a sincerely hard time caring about the story of the game. The plot was mildly interesting, conspiracies and hackers and whatnot, but it didn't land. Mainly because it meant wading through monologues from the characters, which drove me insane. If the game was harder, there would be much more to invest in. I would feel accomplished! But after completing the first two days, I feel like there was no other option but to succeed. There was never any risk of me failing, which made it hard for me to connect to the game at all. In the end it was not the experience I was expecting, and if you're looking to be a tech-savvy sleuth, look elsewhere.

review_text_raw:
I have depression. Playing games is one of a few ways I try to take my mind off of things that would typically worsen that depression, something that is proving exceptionally more difficult at the time of this writing. I actively avoid media that would obviously worsen that depression. I keep up on my anti-depression meds. This is how I take care of myself.

People are free to enjoy the media that they enjoy, and some people will, and have, really enjoyed this game. I won't fault people for that. As much as I hate to say it, I think I'm probably a case study for why some things need content warnings, because I'm going to be carrying this game's ending with me now and I really wish I didn't have to carry that on top of everything else I deal with on a day-to-day basis.

That said, I will not be directly spoiling anything. I went in blind, which if you're like me, I strongly advise you not to do. Watch a playthrough, or preferably just read up on the community posts first. Those'll mostly tell you all you need to know whether this is a game you'll be able to enjoy or not.

All that aside, the investigative gameplay was great, but a little lacking. They introduce tools and mechanics you use once and never again, which feels like a lot of wasted potential.

Again, if you're like me and prefer to play games to escape having to dwell on all the problems with real life, I advise you to give this game a pass and instead, pick up Scrutinized and play it on Detective Mode. Similar gameplay without reminding you quite as much about how much you really hate some aspects of the world you live in.

I think if I weren't in the mental state I'm in, I probably would have enjoyed the game more, and even appreciated the ending more. It is certainly realistic. It wraps up exactly how I would expect this scenario to end in the real world. I think that's why I hate it. It's just reaffirmation that good things don't actually happen to good people. Something I was already well aware of, and really didn't need a reminder.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Short and fun little deep state conspiracy game [/h1] 

First of all, this game is short.[b] VERY SHORT [/b]. It takes about 3-4 hours to complete, but the game tells the story it wants to tell in that time so it´s fine. 

[h3] Story 7/10 [/h3] 
The story is fine. It starts of strong, leaving you as the operator to figure out what you are doing and why you are doing it.
As soon as the story picks up the pace, the game is beginning to get more and more predictable. Sure, it makes sure to tell the story in a convincing way, but if the player has had any contact with books that follow similar plotlines or watched a few "rogue agent fighting conspiracy" movies you know where the plot is going and how the game will end. Ending was fine, a bit disappointing because the cut was fast and hard and resulted in a cliff hanger. To me it feels like the devs wrote a story thats about 10 hours long and just cut the game in half when they had the opportunity to do so, preparing the player for a future sequel.

[b] STORY SPOILERS [/b]
[spoiler] In my opinion the reveal that Mike Trench, our friend and FDI director, is the mole and head of the "Operator Program" was very predictable about half-way through  the game (ever since the Biolab incident and the player operator talking about "baiting out the mole"). The Ghost was written in a very stereotypical bad guy hitman way: I dont have a name, my identity was erased. I know the truth but can not tell you. You can ask any question as long as it is not "out of bounds". Yeah, very corny and kinda cringy. In general, even though the way it is written is good and convincing for the most part, sometimes the game feels like the devs wanted to take the easy way out in a few situations (Player being Sasha Cole, Xavier actually being a friend of HAL, the Ghost just escaping like nothing happened and being able to interfere with HALs scripts...) But hey, for what it is, it´s a solid experience. [/spoiler] 

[h3] Music 7/10 [/h3] 
Pretty good, especially the main menu music. But not memorable. Just nice BGM. Not really worth paying for the OST imo but who am i to decide.

For me the games strong points are the art direction or visual direction in combination with the player interacting with the desktop. It really immerses you in your role as the operator and you really feel like you are investigating CCTV footage and sifting through documents to find small clues. The game really takes you out of this illusion by having to click the objective and then clicking the requested information. Not a fan of that, could have been integrated in a more smooth and immersive way. Audio design is great too, the voice acting feels believable enough and the sound effects are accurate and synced well. Nothing really to complain about there.

Overall it is a fun, short and interesting game with a few flaws that can be overlooked. Wait for a sale before you buy it though, for 3-4 hours of playtime it is just a bit too much (About 1€/$ per hour of playtime should be standard imo).

review_text_raw: I can't in good conscience give this game a good review, but I also can't give it a poor review. It's times like this I wish Steam had a middle-ground review option. This game was very fun and scratched an itch I didn't know I had. However, labeling it as an investigation game or describing it the way it does is misleading. Yes, there is some investigation, but there's really only one singular crime to solve. The storyline is very linear and easy to guess. If it were marketed as a game about solving a singular crime, that would be accurate, but it misleads you in the description by stating, 'Investigate mysterious crimes. Use cutting-edge FDI software to dig for clues, solve puzzles, and uncover the truth.' This is incorrect. You only use most of the 'software' exactly once, after implying you should read the extensive manual that comes along with it. This is a game that you could probably finish within 2-3 hours, which also doesn't justify its price. Honestly, they could have dropped the mid-tier storyline and just made a game along the lines of Criminal Minds or CSI, where you use these tools to try to solve cases, and it would be infinitely more fun. I know I'm probably the outlier here with my review, and I will say I did enjoy what they had, but it just wasn't what they promised in their wording and descriptions (maybe I misunderstood some stuff, who knows). There does seem to be an open door for expansions in the future, but if they're along the same timeframe as this game and offer only 2-3 hours of playtime, they should drastically reduce the price because as it stands, it felt like an expensive tech demo.

6/10 - amazing build-up that doesn't live up to first impression (wish Steam had a neutral as it would have been more realistic); Day 1/2 are 9/10, Day 3/4 are 4/10

PROS:
- atmosphere
- intriguing first half
- feels engaging at early investigations

NEUTRAL:
- game time - on one hand the price is fair for it, but on the other hand the game feels like it's missing bits after about half point mark - which means it would benefit if it was a bit longer
- writing is all over the place ranging from great/clever to cheesy in a bad way (characters especially)

CONS:
- about last third of the game; denouement is abrubt and feels like devs wanted to execute too many points too fast which culminates with general feel of rush writing and ending that just doesn't live up to what ingame Day 1 and 2 have set; investigation results felt like a letdown
- no replay value

It's a solid game that won't be for some people, but for the fans of style, I'd recommend it on sale. Personally, I'm looking forward to their next game as there's so much potential here but also so many opportunities to execute better in their next game. Will follow Bureau 81's future projects.

Okay, while I said I liked this game, [b]I think in terms of recommendation, this is more a "maybe" than an outright "yes."[/b] There are several things to consider before you purchase this one, and while I ultimately think you'll enjoy the experience either way, you may be slightly frustrated by at least one or two of these points. I know I was. 

(-) First, the game is short. It took me less than 4 hours to finish it, and that's with several long cut scenes. Speaking of those cut scenes... pay attention to them. I didn't, because some of them seemed pointless, and that led me to the only time I felt truly stuck in this game LOL.

(+) You play as an operator in the FDI, and the entire gameplay involves sitting in front of your computer, connecting dots, and solving puzzles. I absolutely loved it. It was fresh and interesting, and the feeling of things connecting and unraveling was really fun. I actually wish we had more of it—I would've gladly played more hours of more cases, slowly connecting them to this huge conspiracy. It made me hope that someone would make an entire mystery murder game (as opposed to a conspiracy) as "the guy in the chair," slowly unraveling everything and helping the "heroes" solve the mystery. 

(-/+) For a game that's sitting in front of your computer... the stakes are high and so is the tension. I actually got really anxious at parts, in a way that doesn't really happen with most games because, the way everything is set up, WE are Tenner. So I felt like there was a gun aimed at [i]me[/i] at times, LOL. For me, this was a point in favor of the game, but if you're looking for a more relaxed experience, this may not be it. 

(-/+) The ending. Personally? Not a fan. Oh, I loved the reveal. The minute [i]I[/i] started connecting the dots, my stomach dropped. 10/10 for that. But everything after that?... I will be playing the next game, if there is one, but overall, [spoiler]I am not really the kind of person to enjoy an "everybody died" ending. After all the brilliant puzzle solving, I wanted these characters to have a good ending. I have seen people talk about how this was actually a good ending - how Hal is still thwarting the organization 30 years later, and that's realistic and optimistic but damn. I got attached to [i]these[/i] characters. I wanted to see them happy, even if we fail to totally crush the bad guys in the end of the game. And I wanted to understand what the goal of the "bad guys" in this game is, and I don't. They're evil people, but... why are they doing what they're doing? No clue. Which is another thing I don't like. For me, a game needs to be able to stand on its own, even if it's part of a larger narrative. [/spoiler] Essentially, this felt like a game meant to [i]set up[/i] another game, and truthfully, I don't like that.

So here's a recent and what I consider accurate short review.

The game is worth playing and given it's a bit over the length of a regular movie maybe 2 I'd say at the price of 15 - 25 it's reasonable given movie ticket and popcorn. Replay value isn't really there unless you forget what happened and replay a few years later, but who knows!

It's not really an investigation game and while I'm fine with linear games it is important to mention the plot largely is linear and the actions you can take are too. It's generous with the help in most cases too. It's more like an interactable movie from the main interface of a computer.

The plot and such isn't anything too crazy if you've seen Bourne and Mission Impossible and stuff like that, but it's a pretty good one.

The bomb segment is probably the best part, but it is an absolutely shame that the defusal process is NOT random but instead always the same thing. They had so much information for alternative bombs after all. The ending is highly depressing and ultimately doesn't make a lot of sense due to the wiping the servers and such. I think it should have kept that held back for a potential sequel.

I'd of liked more investigation options, more possibilities to really need to assess things. But I would be interested in a sequel or another game expanding on the systems.

Is it worth a purchase? Yes. And it does really good job at being voluminous in the details and subject matter that they're going into, sometimes a bit too confusingly haha. Whether that's technobabble or someone knew what they were writing about is hard to say. And the voice acting is solid too.

Makes no sense the agents don't have a partner with them at all times tho.

--- I recommend this purchase as a story focused gamer.
Other games you might want to consider that I've played recently that are also story focused or just good: Escape Simulator, Hades, Operation Tango, 	The Operator (this one), Roottree (tho it's less like a game), StarCraft 2 especially Legacy, We Were Here series sequels (but it can be hard at times), Ixion, Strange Horticulture, and a few others.

Thanks for reading --- February 2025.

Edit: As a side note, while the developer seems very pleased with its soundtrack there were a lot of times I didn't really hear any music going on which seemed a bit odd, like during the first server room pursuit to reveal some data.

review_text_raw:
If you want to feel like you're an investigator for the US government in an agency like the FBI or CIA, this game puts you there. It's more than a visual novel, but less than a full-fledged world with practically infinite choices.

Even so, it feels full and like the choices matter. Definitely some memorable moments in this. I would like a full-fledged game with many choices and outcomes, but that would deserve a higher price tag. This is what it should be for the price, and isn't too short.

The story is solid and engaging. Having worked in the government, I can say this is idealized a bit, but is definitely not ridiculous compared to crime shows. I was surprised at several points in the plot, and the way you discover the protagonist's situation and that he encounters is solid.

However, there are a few things that make it a bit realistic. It is set in the early 90s, yet the "FDI" (not FBI) have the capability to "enhance" photos like Stable Diffusion can now. There are cell phone towers and tracking, but not many people used cell phones in the US back at that time, and the ones that did had big Motorolla boxes the size of a lunch box they plugged into. They were technically mobile, but not very. The cell phone antenna had to be attached to the car roof with a magnet. And it cost over $100/mth. Sure, it wasn't uncommon for business people, and really rich people had somewhat smaller mobile phones, but still.

Also, in the boot screen, it shows a version of Linux that is "x86_64", but 64 bit didn't become really common until around 2007.

However, you can forgive these small foibles since you can consider the game as a parallel universe world; very similar, but slightly different, like how you work for the FDI instead of FBI. Perhaps in this world, they had a decade or two jump on us in technology.

I thoroughly enjoyed this and hope they put out a longer game with either more choice or perhaps getting to play more characters, or a single protagonist through a longer story arc. When it comes down to it, my only complaint with this game is that there wasn't more of it. That's a good complaint to have if it matches up with a good price, and it does. Good luck to the dev team now and in the future!

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 98:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆ (8/10)

[i] The Operator [/i] casts you not as a hero in the field, but as the analyst—the voice behind the computer—supporting agents from the shadows. It’s a fascinating setup and a fresh twist on crime-solving games, and usually almost always lives up to its potential!

🖥[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Authentic "operator" fantasy. You monitor missions from your desk, field phone calls, look through mysterious documents, and scrub through CCTV footage. 

[*] Diverse tools. The game gives you a chem scanner, facial recognition database, image enhancement tech, and document search systems. For example, in one mission, you identify a suspect by cross-referencing a blurry security camera with an equally blurry security footage of his car and license plate. That kind of detective work feels cool. You feel smart when it works.

[*] Great use of puzzles under pressure. A standout moment has you guiding a field agent through bomb defusal. You have to analyze chemicals, check your reference files, and read out step-by-step instructions—all while the timer ticks down. These time-sensitive missions are where the game shines.

[*] Well-done audio design. The UI clicks, radio static, and phone calls all contribute to a grounded, late-'90s thriller vibe. The voice acting is low-key but sells the scenario well, especially during moments of stress or confusion.

[*] No filler. It’s tight and focused. No wandering, no padding. You’re thrown into the action quickly and missions move at a brisk pace.
[/list]

[b]🧾 Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Flat characters. The field agents and mysterious hacker HAL are more archetypes than flesh-and-blood. They push the story forward, but rarely surprise

[*] Choices don’t matter much. There are dialogue branches, but most are cosmetic. Whether you’re professional or snarky, or even whether you succeed or fail at certain puzzles, the game mostly funnels you into the same story beats.

[*] Abrupt ending. The game ends just as things get interesting. HAL’s storyline ramps up, then vanishes. You barely get to dig into the conspiracy or see the consequences of your actions. It feels like a miniseries that ends on episode three.
[/list]

Let's start with the obvious as soon as you start the game : the sound design, musics, sound effects, ambiance and voice acting are *gorgeous*. And it gets better with time.

Yet I'm debating to put a thumb up or down. On the one hand, it's original and well made with an impressive level of finition. On pretty much every aspect.
On the other hand ... I don't believe a game is the proper vector for this experience. The gaming aspects constantly break the immersion (at least for me), which in turn ruin any tension or engagement towards the plot, as I view it from a game point of view. For instance, you're in a conversation with someone, yet can take the time to do whatever background checks you want and the person will kindly wait as long as you want before you answer. All of this make the events less impactful emotionnally. I'd add to that a deep insatisfaction with the ending (not as much the content of it as the unfinished business that stops abruptly), and the frustration of sometimes not doing the things right, but still having to deal with the consequences. Yes, it's more immersive, but it makes the gaming experience more frustrating, and I don't want to restart the whole game, so I have a feeling of unfinished business. Not in a branching story game way, more like losing a level but having to go on instead of restarting.

To sum up in a single sentence : the gaming aspects are in the way of the immersion, and the immersion is in the way of the gaming enjoyment.

+++ Sound design
++ Global quality and realism
+ A few good ideas and tools thrown into the mix for variety
- The end, with multiple untied ends
- Too short, with a lack of reusability of the tools and 'sandbox' aspect (you're very handheld at all times)
-- The inadequate mix of immersion and gaming

I bought this game hoping to find a Spycraft (1996) successor, after already beating the two Orwell games, and liking them, but hungry for a more realistic Cold War setting. In a way I was satisfied by The Operator, even if it is a really short game and consequently some story elements are rather simplistic and not well furthered. Some investigation tools are rather cool to use, but unfortunately, for the major part, you use them just once. Some sequences are very tense, like a bomb defusal where you need to read an operative manual and defuse the explosive in 20 minutes. Or another one where you give directions to an agent on the field while looking through a surveillance camera system. But you can't fail at them, this is not an hard game and you just need to solve the puzzles in a linear way to proceed further into the story. Which is not really strong or particulary original, but I liked the final plot twist, which saved it for me exactly when I started to feel bored and uninterested.

As you can see, for every aspect of the game I liked, there is something else I found underwhelming. It is not a bad game but I don't think it can reach the first Orwell game or my favorite title in this genre, Spycraft, from nearly 30 years ago. I will give it a 6, and recommend it anyway, because I would like to see more games in this genre and historical period. Maybe the author will be able to work on a sequel and refine some aspects of it. Meanwhile I'll wait for a real Spycraft successor, let's hope I don't have to wait for another 30 years :|

The Operator — Quick Review

Platform: PC (Steam)

Genre: Puzzle / Simulation / Mystery

Verdict: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ A standout puzzle experience

---

What It Is

The Operator puts you in the role of a remote operator—essentially a digital detective working through cases from behind a screen. You dig through databases, analyze evidence, make phone calls, and piece together mysteries using a realistic desktop interface. It's the kind of game that makes you feel like you're actually doing the job.

Why It Works

The puzzle design is the star. The game doesn't hold your hand. You're given tools, a case file, and just enough rope to figure things out yourself. The satisfaction of connecting two pieces of evidence you found hours apart is genuinely rewarding. It respects your intelligence in a way few puzzle games do.

The interface feels authentic. The fake desktop OS, the clunky database searches, the phone calls—it all adds to the immersion. You're not just solving puzzles; you're inhabiting a role.

The layered structure keeps it fresh. Each case builds on what you've learned, but introduces new mechanics or twists so it never feels repetitive. By the time you've played "a couple layers" (as you put it), the game has opened up into something much deeper than it first appears.

The Vibe

It's methodical. Deliberate. If you want fast-paced action, this isn't it. But if you enjoy the slow burn of untangling a mystery—cross-referencing names, verifying alibis, catching contradictions—The Operator is incredibly satisfying.

Bottom Line

One of the better puzzle experiences on Steam right now. It trusts the player, delivers great "aha!" moments, and wraps it in a polished, believable package. Highly recommended if you enjoy games like Papers, Please, Orwell, or Return of the Obra Dinn.

I absolutely loved The Operator. From the moment I stepped into Evan Tanner’s shoes, booting up that simulated desktop and diving into the role of a rookie operator at the Federal Department of Intelligence, I was hooked. The game didn’t just pull me into its world—it immersed me in a labyrinth of conspiracies, moral dilemmas, and surveillance, all wrapped in a retro ‘90s aesthetic with tech that felt eerily futuristic. It was nostalgic, yes, but also unsettling in the best way.

The gameplay was simple on the surface, but each task—analyzing grainy footage, cross-referencing databases, solving puzzles—made me feel like a true digital detective. It reminded me of Her Story, but stood firmly on its own legs with a tighter narrative and a mystery that grew darker and more complex with every click. The writing was spot-on, and the voice acting had a realism that drew me even deeper into the cases.

Honestly, my biggest gripe was that it ended too soon. I finished it in just a few hours, and while every minute was satisfying, I found myself wishing for more—more time in that richly constructed world, more twists, more layers. The cliffhanger at the end didn’t just tease a continuation; it practically begged for one. I’m really hoping Bureau 81 brings us a sequel that picks up right where the story left off.

Short as it was, The Operator delivered one of the most engaging and rewarding detective experiences I’ve played in ages. It made me pay attention, think critically, and trust my instincts. And I’d jump at the chance to return to that world the moment a sequel drops.

I really don't know how to rate this game. If steam had a "Neutral" option i would have definitely selected that.
With the strict "Yes" or "No" system, I'll hesitantly go for a positive review.

Let's start with the good: It's a really fun game with an interesting story and really good gameplay. The puzzles were interesting and pretty creative. The voice acting was well done and the UI felt nice to use. 
Also, unlike most other games like this, this game does at least try to be accurate with it's technology. Some creative liberties are taken, but as a technically minded person I wasn't screaming "That's not how that works!" all the time.

Now for my main issue: This game is way too short for the price. The game took me 4 hours and that was without trying to go fast. If I tried I feel like this game could be 100% in less that 3 hours (maybe even <2h).
It's not a full $60 game, but even for $15 this is just too short. And the story ends right as it starts getting interesting. Right after some actual intrigue is revealed the credits roll.
Another issue is that it's very linear. It doesn't matter what you do, there is only a single ending. The different options only affect which 10 second response you'll get and nothing after that.

I don't think it's worth getting this game for the full price, but if it's for sale for <$10 it's an alright deal.

The Operator is an incredibly immersive first-person game where you step into the shoes of an FDI operator, guiding field agents through tense, high-stakes situations. The game hooks you with its realistic atmosphere, detailed calls, and the way it makes you feel like a vital part of every operation.

At first, you're focused on supporting agents in their day-to-day missions, but as the game progresses, strange and unsettling elements start creeping into your calls. What begins as routine work grows into a gripping, larger-than-life case that pulls you in emotionally and mentally. The story escalates masterfully, and the twists near the end are nothing short of mind-blowing.

While the gameplay is phenomenal, the only downside is its brevity. The main story can be completed in about 3-4 hours, and there isn’t much replay value since the narrative is linear. Personally, I adore this game, but I really wish it had an endless mode with randomized calls or some kind of story expansion to dive deeper into the experience.

That said, The Operator delivers a thrilling, unforgettable ride. For what it is, it’s a masterpiece—and I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone looking for a unique and engaging game. Here's hoping the developers expand on this concept in the future!

[h2]The Operator[/h2]

There's a specific kind of satisfaction in being handed a suite of official-looking software and told to go find the truth. The Operator gets that feeling exactly right. You sit at your FDI terminal running facial recognition, pulling phone records, cross-referencing databases, and matching evidence, and the tools are just fiddly and authentic enough that every solved case feels like [i]you[/i] cracked it rather than the game waving you through. Nothing lands harder than dragging two pieces of evidence together on a hunch and watching the system confirm you were right.

What surprised me is how well the story holds it all up. The FMV performances could have been cheesy but they're played straight enough to sell a conspiracy that keeps widening in ways I didn't see coming, and the whole thing is wrapped in a moody, convincingly bureaucratic atmosphere that makes a desk job feel tense. It's not a long game, but it's a tight one, and it never overstays its welcome. [b]Recommended[/b], especially if you like detective work that actually makes you think instead of just clicking the obvious next thing.

- It's a pretty good on a technical level. It's a reasonably accurate portrayal of someone working security, albeit with some obvious creative liberties taken.
- The music was great

Cons:
- It's shorter than you'd think
- There are some parts that were confusing.
- The hints felt like you were being talked down to.

Compare and contrast with, say, The Root Trees are Dead, which is a bit different, but it has similar detective vibes. RTaD felt like you were peeling back layers of an onion to find the secrets buried in a mountain of info. The Operator felt like you were in an onion peeling factory that had you operate cool machines, but treated like you were dumb for not knowing which nob made middle onion layers go off.

I didn't want to hit the thumbs down this because it is worth your time, but maybe not $10 worth of time.

It's like an interactive movie and I love it! Haven't played a mystery puzzle game this satisfying for a while. Of course I don't know exactly how the real FBI does things, but the game mechanics felt very authentic and polished. It established that "can't trust anyone" vibe so well I was on the edge of my seat towards the very end not knowing who is on my side. The music was used well both in terms of timing to bring tensity up at important plot points. Frequency of using these soundtracks were on point too so as to not break immersion. I'll agree the ending felt slightly rushed and didn't feel like proper closure, but after watching the post-credits, I'll gladly take it as a cliffhanger and a bait for the sequel.

If you are a fan of Obra Dinn or Case of the Golden Idol, you will especially love this!

- Interactive research mechanics: dive deep into case files, interview witnesses, and analyze evidence
- Innovative investigation system: follow leads, connect dots, and solve crimes
- Challenging puzzles: keep you on the edge of your seat

Pros:

- High replayability
- Realistic investigation mechanics
- Engaging storyline

Cons: None notable

If you're a fan of investigative games or looking for a unique gaming experience, "The Operator" is a must-play.

Highly Recommended!

Overall, I enjoyed my time with it, but I do not think I will ever replay it.

A fun, tense, short (maybe 3 hours) console simulator along the lines of games like Orwell or Greyhat. You won't be doing any actual hacking, and apart from a few mini-games much of the game is just you poking around a computer and sliding into other people's DMs.

But this short game packs a lot of tension and twists through a clean interface and fantastic voice actors. Definitely worth a try if you're a fan of this style of story!
